lead: Rocky Mountain oysters are skinned, deep-fried bull testicles. Some men eat them as a traditional virility food, believing they support their own testosterone, masculine looks and drive.

The dish is tied to ranching and cattle castration, and many people consider it an aphrodisiac. The usual belief is a "like supports like" transfer of benefit from organ to eater; no studies were found testing a hormonal effect.

paras: It is eaten as a food, usually fried and served as a regional dish or specialty, or as part of a nose-to-tail organ-meat diet. People who eat it for testosterone typically make it an occasional meal.
No specific risks are described in the sources reviewed. As with any meat, safety depends on how it is sourced and cooked.

angle.text: Some men eat Rocky Mountain oysters as a traditional virility food, expecting it to support their testosterone, masculine drive and looks. The practice comes from folklore, and no human data on testosterone were found.

lead: Eating testicles, often as Rocky Mountain oysters, is the practice of consuming animal testicles in the belief that they support male hormones or virility. People in ancestral-diet, bodybuilding and manosphere communities eat them, cooked or raw, with the aim of raising testosterone, which they associate with more muscle, leaner body composition and a more masculine look.[1][2][3] Rocky Mountain oysters are a dish of bulls' testicles, usually skinned and deep-fried.[1]

The dish is traditionally associated with ranching and cattle castration, and many people consider it an aphrodisiac.[1] The idea that eating an organ strengthens the matching organ in the eater is an old one, and in recent years it has been revived by online personalities. The Liver King, a YouTube personality who promotes an ancestral diet, was shown in a 2025 Netflix documentary eating bull testicles with his family, and coverage reported the family eating them three times a day to raise testosterone.[3] In 2024 a Florida man known as John drew attention for a video series about eating raw bull testicles daily to test the claim.[4]

Commentators have reported that no scientific studies on the question have been found. Pharmacologist Joe Graedon of The People's Pharmacy wrote that he doubted cooked mountain oysters would deliver a pharmacological dose of the hormone.[5] No clinical studies were found testing whether eating testicles changes human testosterone.
infobox: Prairie oysters, calf fries, criadillas, huevos de toro[1]

paras: Rocky Mountain oysters are bull testicles that are skinned, coated in seasoned flour and deep-fried, and are sometimes pounded flat first.[1] Regional names include prairie oysters in Canada, calf fries in Oklahoma and the Texas Panhandle, and criadillas in Spain, Argentina and much of Mexico. Similar dishes use lamb, pig or turkey testicles.[1] Freeze-dried testicle capsules are also sold as supplements.

The dish is described as purported cowboy fare tied to ranching families; the culinary use is a by-product of livestock castration. Several US towns hold testicle festivals, including Eagle, Idaho, and Virginia City, Nevada. Many people regard it as an aphrodisiac.[1]

sections.h: Use in ancestral-diet and manosphere communities
paras: Brian Johnson, known as the Liver King, promotes a diet of raw red meat, daily liver and bull testicles. He admitted in 2022 to steroid use after a leak of emails, and a May 2025 Netflix documentary, Untold: The Liver King, shows his family killing a bull and eating its testicles. Coverage of the documentary reported that the family eats bull testicles three times a day to boost testosterone and noted that they contain little testosterone.[3] T Nation members have discussed the Liver King's content in forum threads.[6]

In June 2024 a Florida man known as John, who had earlier eaten raw chicken daily for 100 days, announced he would test the belief that organ meats, especially testicles, take you to the next level by eating raw bull testicles daily. He had not reported specific physical changes at the time of the coverage.[4]

Joe Graedon of The People's Pharmacy wrote that he could not find any scientific studies devoted to the question and doubted a pharmacological dose of the hormone would come from cooked mountain oysters.[5] Coverage of the Netflix documentary similarly noted that bull testicles contain little testosterone.[3] Raw organ meat in general carries foodborne illness risks, which commentators have raised in connection with the raw-testicle trend.[4]

A 2019 study of beef variety meats measured vitamin K forms called menaquinones (MK4 to MK13) in raw and cooked organ meats, because animal-derived menaquinones had been poorly characterised.[2] This concerns vitamin K content, not testosterone.

lore.intro: Testicle eating appears in ancestral-diet and testosterone-focused communities as a food said to support male hormones, and in forum threads about the Liver King.[3][4][6]
